lesson.title: Everything Is a Resource: The Architecture Behind Modern APIs
lesson.summary: REST is not a protocol but an architectural style for designing web APIs around resources, identified by URLs and manipulated using standard HTTP methods, with no session state stored on the server between requests.
lesson.body:
REST, short for Representational State Transfer, is a set of design principles for building APIs on top of HTTP, first described by Roy Fielding in his 2000 doctoral dissertation. It is worth being precise that REST is not itself a protocol the way HTTP or TCP are. It is an architectural style, a way of organizing an API so that it uses HTTP the way HTTP was actually designed to be used, rather than treating HTTP as a generic tunnel for passing arbitrary function calls back and forth.

The central idea is that everything an API exposes is modeled as a resource, a noun, addressed by a URL. A book, a user account, an order, a comment: each of these gets its own URL, like /books/17 or /users/42. What you want to do to that resource is expressed through the HTTP method, not through the URL itself. GET /books/17 retrieves the book. PUT /books/17 replaces it entirely. PATCH /books/17 updates part of it. DELETE /books/17 removes it. POST /books creates a new book inside the books collection. This is a real departure from an older, more common style where the URL itself encodes the action, like /getBook?id=17 or /deleteBook?id=17. In that older style, the verb is baked into the URL and the HTTP method is often just POST or GET regardless of what is actually happening; in REST, the URL names a thing and the HTTP method says what to do to it.

The second defining property of REST is statelessness. Every request from a client to a server must contain all the information the server needs to understand and process it, such as an authentication token, and the server does not keep any session state about that client hanging around in memory between requests. This has real consequences for how systems scale: because no server needs to remember anything about a particular client from one request to the next, any server in a cluster behind a load balancer can handle any incoming request, which makes it far easier to add more servers and distribute load without worrying about which server a client's previous requests happened to land on.

REST also leans on the parts of HTTP that already existed for exactly this purpose, rather than reinventing them. Standard HTTP status codes communicate outcomes, a 200 for success, a 404 when a resource does not exist, a 201 when something new was created. HTTP's caching mechanisms can be used directly, since GET requests to a resource URL are naturally cacheable. And REST is not tied to any particular version of HTTP; a RESTful API can run over HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2, or HTTP/3 without changing anything about its design, because REST describes how resources and methods are organized, not which transport carries the bytes.
